contributions.headingText: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant polyp and cancer predisposition syndrome characterized by mucocutaneous melanin pigmentation and gastrointestinal polyposis, associated with STK11 mutation.
Cervix and ovary, gastrointestinal tract, breast, skin, and lung

PJS is associated with a moderate or high risk of a range of malignancies, with an overall risk of any cancer by the age of 70 years of 81% (see #15233Table #15233) {16707622; 11113065; 3587280}. Tumours of the female genital tract include cervical gastric-type mucinous adenocarcinoma and sex cord tumour with annular tubules (SCTAT) and much less commonly Sertoli cell tumours of the ovary. Other extraintestinal tumours include carcinomas of the breast and pancreas, as well as Sertoli cell tumour of the testis. PJS patients with gastric-type mucinous adenocarcinoma are younger (mean age: 33 years) than non-syndromic patients {24179492}. SCTATs occur in the second and third decades of life {29373116}.

Presenting symptoms include abdominal pain, intestinal bleeding, anaemia, and intussusception, which typically manifest in the first two decades of life {17311531}. If present, the characteristic mucocutaneous pigmentation allows diagnosis of asymptomatic patients in familial cases, but the characteristic Peutz–Jeghers polyps are the main clinical hallmark. The uterine cervical tumours are associated with abnormal vaginal bleeding and watery discharge {29233547}. The ovarian tumours may be an incidental finding or may present with signs and symptoms related to a pelvic mass {15644771}.

The prevalence of PJS is 1 case per 50 000–200 000 births {16616343}. The cumulative risk of cervical gastric-type mucinous adenocarcinoma is 10% and of ovarian tumours 21% {16616343}. PJS is implicated in 10% of all cervical gastric-type mucinous adenocarcinomas and 36% of all SCTATs {24179492}.

An inherited germline mutation of the tumour suppressor gene STK11 (chromosome 19p13.3) is implicated in > 90% of cases {9428765; 24179492; 16287113}. Most germline defects are point mutations and small intragenic deletions, but larger deletions of one or more exons have also been described {17924967}.

The direct precursor to gastrointestinal cancer in patients with PJS remains unknown {16344569}. Peutz–Jeghers polyps are probably an epiphenomenon to the cancer-prone condition and not obligate malignant precursors {16344569; 21940722}. There are no data on the pathogenesis of breast or female genital tumours.

Cervical tumours are often indurated, barrel-shaped, and centred in the transformation zone {2764221}. SCTATs are often not grossly visible, although they may form bilateral visible yellow nodules {7104978; 29373116}, while Sertoli cell tumours typically form a solid mass with a yellow cut surface {15644771}.

Cervical gastric-type mucinous adenocarcinoma encompasses a spectrum ranging from well-differentiated (minimal deviation) to overtly malignant tumours {17460448; 29233547; 26685087}. Lobular endocervical glandular hyperplasia also occurs in PJS, including atypical forms, and is considered a precursor to gastric-type mucinous adenocarcinoma {23038761; 29233547}. Rarely, synchronous metaplastic and neoplastic mucinous lesions may occur in the endometrium, fallopian tube, ovary, peritoneum, bladder, and intestine in this setting {7977943; 27550049; 19207943}. SCTATs in syndromic patients are typically bilateral and multifocal, and they are often accompanied by microcalcifications {7104978}, in contrast to non-syndromic neoplasms {29373116; 7104978}. Sertoli cell tumours may be oxyphilic or lipid-rich {15644771}.

Refer also to the Histopathology subsections in section Adenocarcinoma, HPV-independent, gastric type, of the uterine cervix and section Sex cord tumour with annular tubules.
Essential: fulfilment of the clinical diagnostic criteria for PJS.
Staging is the same as for other cervical and ovarian tumours.

Gastric-type mucinous adenocarcinoma is associated with aggressive behaviour and poor outcome {26457350}. In contrast, SCTATs are associated with an excellent prognosis {7104978}. Sertoli cell tumours may rarely be malignant. Tumour surveillance guidelines recommend annual cervical cytology and transvaginal ultrasound {16616343; 27241107}.
